- **Line contact instead of surface contact.** Each jar now touches the floor along a single line and touches the board along a single line directly above it. The contact width is effectively zero, so there is almost nothing resisting sideways motion.
- **It is a roller, and rolling is free.** A cylinder lying on a flat surface is in *neutral* equilibrium about its rolling axis: there is no restoring force at all. Rolling resistance for smooth glass on the smooth enamelled sheet-metal floor seen here is negligible, and the floor is visibly wet/stained in places, which makes it worse. So there is no "it will hold unless you push hard" — any horizontal force whatsoever, however small, makes the jars roll and the board translate.
- **A plank on three rollers is a cart.** The board is no longer pinned in place; it becomes free to slide along the direction the jars can roll. Loading the cheese moulds onto it, the swing of the cabinet door, a bump against the appliance, or vibration from the fan/element in the top of the box would all be enough to set it moving, and once the board translates the jars roll out from under its edges and everything comes down.
- **Real jars are not perfect cylinders, so they will not even roll straight.** Mason jars taper slightly at the shoulder and neck, carry a proud threaded band at the mouth, and have a raised heel ring at the base. Lying on its side, a jar therefore rests on two rings of slightly different diameter — mildly cone-like — so it rolls in an arc rather than a straight line, and it will steadily wander off course rather than staying put. It also means the three top tangent lines are not guaranteed to be at exactly the same height, so the board would sit very slightly cocked.
- **Aligning them is finicky.** For the board to sit level at all, the three jars would have to be laid with their axes parallel and at matched heights. Get that right and you have made a roller conveyor; get it wrong and the board rocks on three points at different heights.

## Two secondary consequences

- **The shelf drops.** The support height stops being the jar's height and becomes its diameter — from roughly 105–113 px down to roughly 75–81 px in the image, i.e. the shelf would sit about 30% lower, some 3–4 cm down.
- **It would probably land on the hose.** The red flexible tube already runs through the space under the board, and its upper edge sits only about 20 px below the board's underside on the right-hand side. Dropping the board by ~30 px would bring it down onto that tubing, which would either squash the hose or tilt the board — and a round, soft hose contributes nothing useful as a support.

## Verdict

If you set everything up with infinite care on a perfectly level surface and then never touched it, three jars on their sides could momentarily hold a bamboo board up — statics allows it, and the glass is in no danger of breaking. But that is balancing, not supporting. Because a cylinder on its side has no resistance to rolling and only line contact top and bottom, the arrangement has zero margin against disturbance, whereas the upright jars in the photo have plenty. Inside a cabinet with a swinging door, a fan, a hose underneath and a few kilos of cheese being lifted on and off the shelf, the flipped version would roll apart. So: the glasses would still be *able* to carry the weight, but they would no longer *hold the shelf up* in any usable way.

But a glass lying on its side is a roller. It has nothing to stop it rolling, so the shelf would have no stable support and would shift, drop off the glasses or collapse at the slightest disturbance. ## What the picture shows

The photo is of a small refrigerator that has been turned into a cheese cave. On the fridge floor stand three straight-sided glass jars (they look like canning or jelly jars, apparently turned upside down so the mouth is on the floor and the flat base is on top). A bamboo cutting board lies across the tops of the three jars and serves as a shelf. On the board are two cheese wheels, a red container, a small digital thermometer/hygrometer and a mesh strainer. A red tube runs along the floor and up under the board between the jars. Small black pegs on the side walls sit at shelf height and touch the ends of the board. They may stop it sliding sideways, but they do not carry its weight; the jars do.

## Why the upright jars work

- Standing on end, each jar meets the floor with a flat rim and meets the board with a flat base. Flat-on-flat contact gives a wide footprint. A sideways nudge produces a restoring effect and the jar simply stays where it is.
- The weight travels straight down the jar walls in compression, the direction in which glass is extremely strong.
- Three well-spaced jars give the board three solid, fixed bearing points, so it does not rock and cannot slide.

## What changes when the jars lie on their sides

1. **They become rollers.** A jar on its side touches the floor along one line and touches the board along one line. Nothing resists rolling. A level board on level, identical cylinders is only in neutral equilibrium: it does not fall on its own, but it also has nothing pulling it back if it moves. Any horizontal push, a slightly tilted board, weight placed off-centre when cheese is put on, vibration from the compressor, or the door being closed will make one or more jars roll out from under the board, and the shelf drops.
2. **Point or line contacts replace flat contacts.** Because the jars have a slightly raised rim/thread ring at one end, they would not even lie perfectly flat; each would rest on the ring and tip slightly, so the board would touch each jar at roughly a single high point. Balancing a loaded board on three such points is precarious. Ordinary tapered drinking glasses would be worse still, since a tapered glass lies as a tilted cone and rolls in a circle.
3. **The shelf would sit much lower.** A jar on its side is only as tall as its diameter, roughly two-thirds of its standing height, so the board would drop noticeably. It would then no longer line up with the black wall pegs, losing even that lateral restraint, and it would come down onto the red tube that runs under it, which would prop the board up unevenly and add to the tilt that sets the jars rolling.
4. **Strength is not the problem.** Lying down, a jar carries the load across its diameter, bending the glass wall (hoop stress) rather than compressing it along its length. That is a weaker way to load glass, but the board plus a few small cheeses is only a few kilograms, so a jar would carry its share without cracking, especially if the board is placed gently. The jars would not break; they would roll.

## Conclusion

Placed gently on a level floor, three jars on their sides could hold the board up for a moment, because glass is strong enough and a level board on level cylinders is in equilibrium. That is not real support. Round glasses lying on their sides roll freely, so the shelf would be unstable, would sit lower, and would fall as soon as anything disturbed it or the cheese was loaded unevenly. In practical terms the glasses would no longer be able to support the shelf. Standing them on end, as in the photo, is what makes the shelf work.

# Analysis of Supporting a Wooden Shelf with Glasses Resting on Their Sides

Based on the image provided (`/app/media/image.png`), three glass jars (specifically Mason jars) are currently used upside down to support a wooden cutting board, which serves as a shelf inside a cooler/refrigerator.

If the glass jars were flipped so that they rested on their sides (horizontally) rather than vertically, **they would not be able to reliably or stably support the wooden shelf.** 

Here is a detailed physical and geometric analysis of why this is the case:

---

## 1. Mechanical Instability and Rolling
* **The Rolling Problem:** Glass jars are cylindrical. When placed vertically, their flat bases and rims provide stable, flat support surfaces. If flipped onto their sides, they will lie horizontally. On a flat surface, cylinders are free to roll along their curved surfaces. 
* **Lack of Restraint:** Unless there are wedges, blocks, or adhesive to prevent the jars from rolling, any slight horizontal force, vibration, or asymmetric weight distribution on the shelf will cause the jars to roll. This would immediately lead to the shelf tilting, sliding off, and collapsing.
* **Non-Parallel Orientation Limitations:** Even if one were to attempt to arrange the three jars in non-parallel directions (e.g., at angles to each other in a triangle to prevent mutual rolling in a single direction), the system remains highly unstable. The shelf would easily slip or slide off the smooth, curved glass surfaces.

---

## 2. Line Contact vs. Planar Contact
* **Reduced Support Surface:** In their current vertical orientation, the jars make full planar contact (circular contact) with both the floor of the compartment and the underside of the wooden shelf, which distributes the weight and prevents tipping.
* **Line Contact:** When lying horizontally on their sides, the jars only make **line contact** (a single line of contact) with the floor and another line of contact with the shelf. Line contact has extremely low frictional resistance to tipping and sliding, making it virtually impossible to balance a flat board stably on top of them.

---

## 3. Uneven Geometry of Mason Jars
* **Threaded Necks and Tapered Bodies:** Mason jars are not perfect, uniform cylinders. They have raised glass threads and wider rims at their mouths, and they often taper slightly near the neck or base.
* **Uneven Leveling:** When laid on their sides, the jars will not lie perfectly flat or level. Their axes will tilt because the wider rim at the mouth lifts one end higher than the body/base. This unevenness means the wooden shelf would not rest horizontally; it would tilt, causing the items on top (like the cheese wheels) to slide off.

---

## 4. Structural Strength (Compression Dynamics)
* **Axial vs. Radial Loading:** Vertically, glass cylinders are extremely strong because they are loaded axially (compression along the walls), which is the optimal way to support loads. 
* **Radial Compression:** Horizontally, the jars would be subjected to radial/diametral compression. While thick-walled glass jars are strong enough that they would likely not shatter under the gentle weight of a light wooden shelf and cheese, their structural load-bearing capacity is significantly reduced in this horizontal orientation.

---

## Conclusion
While the glass jars might possess the raw material strength to not crush under a very light, gently placed wooden board, they **cannot support the shelf** due to **extreme physical instability, rolling, and uneven geometry**. 
Without external constraints to block them from rolling and sliding, flipping the glasses onto their sides would cause the shelf to collapse.

# Answer: No — on their sides the glasses could not still support the shelf

In this picture I see a light wooden board spanning the full inside width
of a small box-like enclosure with its front door open. Under the board
are three transparent glass mason jars, all inverted and vertical, with
their mouths down on the flat floor and their flat bases up in contact
with the underside of the board. The board carries two solid round cheese
wheels toward the left and centre and a rectangular dish toward the right.
I take the stated premise as confirmed: the three vertical jars are
currently holding the board up, level, with one jar near the left, one near
the middle-rear, and one near the right.

Each jar is visibly taller than it is wide. Its height is roughly one and
one half to two times its diameter, as is normal for a mason jar. Turning
each jar 90 degrees to rest on its cylindrical side would therefore change
the support height from jar height to jar diameter. The board would have to
sit much lower, roughly one half to two thirds of its present height. Even
assuming the board is lowered very gently onto the side-lying jars, they
would not still support it as a stable, level shelf. My answer is
explicitly no.

I state each reason explicitly.

First, stable flat contact would become unstable rolling contact. At
present each jar has a flat circular face on the floor and a flat circular
face against the board, so it cannot roll. On its side each jar is a
near-cylinder with essentially line contact below and line contact above. A
flat board on cylinders is a roller support. It is free to roll sideways
with very little force. Placing the wood gently only avoids knocking the
jars over during placement. It does not remove their freedom to roll after
placement.

Second, friction is low and the load is uneven. The floor appears to be
smooth enamelled metal and the jars are smooth glass, while the board-to-
glass contact is also smooth. The visible load is left-heavy, with two
heavy cheese wheels on the left and centre and a lighter dish on the right.
Any small vibration, slight asymmetry in placement, or offset loading will
start one or more jars rolling. Once one rolls, the board translates or
drops at one corner and the arrangement collapses. Three separate unchocked
rollers do not lock each other.

Third, the rolling directions are dangerous in this box. The front of the
enclosure is open with no lip. If the side-lying jars are placed with their
axes left-right, their rolling direction is front-back, so board and jars
can roll straight out the open front. If they are placed with axes front-
back, their rolling direction is left-right, so the board can shift
sideways until one or more jars no longer bear on it. Neither orientation
is captured.

Fourth, the jars are tapered, not true cylinders. A mason jar body is wider
than its threaded mouth. I can see the threaded mouth rings at the floor
contact in the enlarged view. Lying on its side, each jar would bear on the
wide body at one end and the narrower mouth ring at the other, so its axis
would be tilted and its upper bearing line would be slanted, not
horizontal. Three such tilted jars would not present three equal-height
level bearing lines. The board would be tilted, bear on small high points,
and tend to slide toward the narrow ends. It could not be level as it is
now.

Fifth, transverse loading is weaker than the present axial loading. At
present the weight of board plus cheese is carried in compression along the
glass walls. On the side, the same weight would bear transversely across
the thin curved wall on a narrow line, producing local bending and high
contact stress. That is a less favourable and less reliable way to carry
cheese wheels, in addition to being unstable.

Sixth, the enclosure has fixed side-wall pins at the present board height.
In the enlarged views a black pin protrudes from the right side wall at
essentially the same height as the thickness of the board and meets the
board end, with a matching hole or pin position on the left wall. Those are
the adjustable-shelf pins of the box. The present board height is therefore
the pin height. Side-lying jars are substantially shorter and would not
reach that height, so at the original height they would leave a clear gap
and carry nothing. To use them the board would have to be lowered below the
pins. That would lose whatever lateral location the pins provide to the
full-width board and would require passing a full-width board past
protruding pins.

Seventh, the floor space is already threaded by a red hose or cable that
runs across behind and between the upright jars at roughly one third of
their height. Upright jars have a small round footprint and fit around it.
Side-lying jars would have a long rectangular footprint equal to jar height
in one direction and would have to cross or sit on that hose unless the
hose were moved. Resting partly on a soft round hose would add rocking and
uneven height.

For all of these reasons, and especially the change from flat non-rolling
support to tapered rollers, the side-lying glasses would be lower,
unlevel, free to roll, more highly stressed, disengaged from the designed
shelf height, and in conflict with the hose routing. They might balance for
a moment if placed perfectly gently, but they would not still be able to
support the wooden shelf.
